Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
go along with whatever others want to feel safe
Being reminded of the event by others

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
I feel like an object, not like a person

vignette: Nalani had always been drawn to urban planning because of its promise of order and control. As a child, her world was chaotic and unpredictable - her caregiver's physical abuse left her feeling like she was walking on eggshells, never knowing when the next explosion would come. Even now, at 24, Nalani felt like she was still trying to make sense of that childhood. She had learned to navigate the world with a mix of people-pleasing and avoidance, going along with whatever others wanted to feel safe, while also carefully limiting her interactions to avoid any reminders of the past. But some things were harder to avoid than others. Medical procedures, for instance, made Nalani's stomach turn - the smell of antiseptic, the feeling of being trapped on a table, it all brought back memories she couldn't quite access when she tried to recall them deliberately. She would get nauseous just thinking about it, and her mind would start spinning with counterfactual thoughts - what if she had been born into a different family? What if she had been stronger, or faster, or smarter? Would things have turned out differently? Nalani's job required her to be in public spaces, but being seen made her feel self-conscious, like an object on display. She would find herself scanning the room for potential threats, her heart racing at sudden movements by others. Her colleagues might joke about her "spidey sense," but Nalani knew it was just her body's way of trying to stay safe in a world that still felt hostile. It wasn't just physical spaces that made Nalani feel uneasy - she had difficulty concentrating, and would often find herself zoning out in meetings or while working on projects. She felt like she was constantly on guard, waiting for the other shoe to drop. When memories of the abuse did surface, they brought with them a wave of intense rage - Nalani would feel like she was reliving the event all over again, her emotions raw and overwhelming. Despite her best efforts to avoid reminders, Nalani couldn't shake the feeling that what happened to her was deeply unfair. She felt like an object, not a person - a plaything for someone else's twisted desires. And when she thought about it too much, she would start to feel weak all over again, like she was back in that helpless child's body. Lately, Nalani had started to notice the toll her avoidance strategies were taking on her life. She was turning down projects at work because they required her to interact with too many people, or visit unfamiliar places. Her social life was dwindling, as she found it harder and harder to muster the energy for dates or nights out with friends. It was like she was living in a tiny little world, one that was slowly shrinking. That's when Nalani realized she needed help - not just to cope with her symptoms, but to start building a life that wasn't defined by fear and avoidance. She was scared of what might happen if she started confronting the past, but she was more afraid of staying stuck in this narrow little existence. As she sat in her small apartment, surrounded by maps and blueprints for cities she had never visited, Nalani felt a glimmer of hope - maybe, just maybe, she could start to rebuild herself, one small step at a time.
